reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
clinicalPearls: Paragonimiasis is caused by lung flukes of the genus Paragonimus, chiefly P. westermani, endemic in East and Southeast Asia, with other species in Africa and the Americas
Infection follows eating raw, undercooked or pickled freshwater crabs or crayfish, or in some regions raw meat of paratenic hosts, containing infective metacercariae
After ingestion the larvae penetrate the gut and diaphragm and produce migratory subcutaneous swellings before settling in the lungs to form parasitic cysts
The pulmonary syndrome mimics tuberculosis: chronic cough, chest pain and haemoptysis with rusty-brown or blood-streaked sputum, often in an otherwise well patient
Ectopic (extrapulmonary) disease is important, particularly cerebral paragonimiasis, which can cause seizures, focal deficits and space-occupying lesions
Diagnosis rests on finding the characteristic operculated eggs in sputum or stool, supported by serology, eosinophilia and imaging showing cysts, ring shadows or pleural effusion
Praziquantel is the treatment of choice for paragonimiasis, with corticosteroid cover considered in cerebral disease to limit inflammatory reaction
reference.pathophysiology: Ingested metacercariae excyst in the small intestine, penetrate the intestinal wall into the peritoneal cavity, and migrate through the diaphragm into the pleural space and lungs, where paired adult flukes become enclosed in fibrous cysts that communicate with bronchioles. Eggs are coughed up and either expectorated or swallowed and passed in stool. Local inflammation, cyst formation and rupture into airways produce the chronic cough and haemoptysis, while pleural involvement causes effusion. Aberrant migration of larvae to the brain, subcutaneous tissue, abdomen or other sites produces ectopic disease, with cerebral involvement being the most serious.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary tuberculosis (closely mimicked and often co-endemic)
Bronchiectasis or chronic bacterial lung infection
Other causes of haemoptysis and pleural effusion
Neurocysticercosis or other space-occupying lesions (for cerebral disease)
additionalInvestigations: Microscopy of sputum for characteristic operculated eggs (repeated samples improve yield)
Stool microscopy for swallowed eggs when sputum is negative
Serology (antibody detection), useful especially in ectopic disease and light infection
Chest imaging (radiograph/CT) for cysts, ring shadows, infiltrates or pleural effusion
Brain imaging when cerebral involvement is suspected
redFlags: Neurological features (seizures, focal deficit, raised intracranial pressure) suggesting cerebral paragonimiasis
Large pleural effusion or empyema causing respiratory compromise
Diagnostic confusion with tuberculosis leading to inappropriate anti-TB therapy
reference.prognosis: Pulmonary paragonimiasis usually responds well to anthelmintic therapy with a good outlook, but cerebral and other ectopic disease can leave lasting neurological deficits, and misdiagnosis as tuberculosis often delays effective treatment.
pitfalls: Treating the patient as smear-negative tuberculosis and overlooking lung fluke eggs in sputum
Relying on a single sputum sample, which may miss eggs
Not considering cerebral paragonimiasis in an endemic patient with seizures
Neglecting dietary counselling, allowing reinfection from raw crab or crayfish
Omitting corticosteroid cover in cerebral disease where an inflammatory reaction to dying flukes is a concern
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
